lines.text: So far we have a huge squid, and a whale that eats it. Now let's look closely at the body of the thing.
Colossal squid and giant squid have the biggest eyes of any living animal.
On the 2007 colossal squid, the eyes were measured at around twenty seven centimeters across. That is about the size of a soccer ball.
One caveat. That animal had spent over a year in a freezer, and Te Papa, the New Zealand museum that studied it, says it shrank a little, so the living eye may have been even bigger.
Why would an animal need an eye that big?
Down there, there is almost no light. A 2012 study in the journal Current Biology offered an idea.
The researchers think that a big eye lets a squid spot a sperm whale coming, because the whale stirs up glowing sea life as it swims.
In the right conditions, they calculated, a squid could see that glow from about a hundred and twenty meters away.
Think about that. In the dark, with no sun, the thing that keeps this squid alive might be spotting a whale coming.
So the eye may be a whale alarm.
Now the other end of the animal. Its arms carry hooks, and its two long tentacles carry hooks that can rotate all the way round, a full three hundred and sixty degrees.
Those tentacles are about two meters long.
So here is an animal with enormous eyes in the dark, and a set of rotating hooks.
And all of it, until recently, we had only seen on animals that were dead.
Which brings us to the question. Had anyone ever seen one alive, swimming free in its own world?
